name: Liraglutide

lead: Liraglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist from Novo Nordisk, given as a daily injection. It was approved as Victoza for type 2 diabetes and, at a higher strength, as Saxenda for chronic weight management; it was the first GLP-1 drug approved for obesity treatment.

Its weight-loss effect is more modest than that of semaglutide or tirzepatide, with average losses in trials of roughly 5 to 8 percent of body weight. It is now of mainly historical or niche interest in fat-loss circles, as newer agents with larger reported effects have largely replaced it.

paras: Liraglutide is a GLP-1 analogue with a fatty-acid chain that promotes albumin binding and gives it a half-life of about 13 hours, allowing once-daily dosing. By activating GLP-1 receptors it increases satiety, delays gastric emptying and enhances glucose-dependent insulin release, which lowers calorie intake and body weight.

Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and constipation are the usual complaints, with gallbladder events, pancreatitis and raised heart rate reported less often. It carries a boxed warning about thyroid C-cell tumours in rodents. Weight is commonly regained when the drug is stopped, and it requires daily injections. It is prescription-only.

lead: Liraglutide is a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist made by Novo Nordisk and given by daily subcutaneous injection. Under the brand name Victoza it is used for type 2 diabetes, and at a higher strength as Saxenda it is used for chronic weight management; it is also available as a generic [1][2]. It was approved in the European Union in 2009 and in the United States in 2010 [1].

Its weight-loss effect in trials is smaller than that of the newer weekly drugs semaglutide and tirzepatide. Wikipedia describes liraglutide as less effective than standard-dose semaglutide for weight loss, and the STEP 8 trial compared the two directly [1][3]. In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums it is discussed mostly as an older, shorter-acting alternative that some users prefer because the daily schedule lets them time doses [4].

The US label has a boxed warning about thyroid C-cell tumors seen in rodents, and other labelled risks include pancreatitis, hypoglycemia with some other diabetes drugs, and acute kidney injury from volume depletion [2].

paras: Victoza is indicated as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in people aged ten and over with type 2 diabetes, and to reduce major adverse cardiovascular events in adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease [1][2]. Saxenda is indicated with a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity for long-term weight reduction in people aged twelve and over with obesity and a body weight above 60 kg, and in adults with overweight and a weight-related condition [1]. American Diabetes Association guidance cited by Wikipedia considers it a first-line option for people with type 2 diabetes and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or obesity [1].

Appearance-focused users take liraglutide to lose body fat through appetite suppression. As with other GLP-1 drugs, it is not known to affect facial fat selectively; any facial change follows overall fat loss. Forum posters mention it as a cheaper or lower-intensity option than semaglutide, with some saying that peptide sites sell liraglutide [4][5].

In the SCALE trial, 3,731 people with obesity or overweight and no type 2 diabetes received liraglutide 3.0 mg or placebo for 56 weeks [6]. A separate SCALE Diabetes trial tested the same dose in people with type 2 diabetes [7], and a 3-year trial tested it in people with prediabetes for diabetes risk reduction and weight management [8]. In the head-to-head STEP 8 trial, weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg was compared with daily liraglutide 3.0 mg over 68 weeks [3]. Wikipedia states liraglutide led to greater weight loss than some earlier GLP analogues but less than standard-dose semaglutide [1].

A 2025 network meta-analysis of body composition found that liraglutide was the only GLP-1 agonist in that analysis to produce significant weight reduction without a significant reduction in lean mass, though the analysis was across heterogeneous trials [9]. Another randomized trial examined combining exercise with a GLP-1 agonist on metabolic syndrome and abdominal obesity [10]. A 2025 meta-analysis of GLP-1 drugs examined weight after discontinuation [11].

Common effects include nausea, dizziness, abdominal pain, injection-site pain and low blood sugar when combined with other glucose-lowering drugs. Gastrointestinal effects are strongest at the start of treatment and tend to subside [1]. Serious effects listed include angioedema, pancreatitis, gallbladder disease and kidney problems [1]. The label warns about thyroid C-cell tumors in rodents, which is a boxed warning, and says it is unknown whether liraglutide causes such tumors in humans [2]. Wikipedia notes that in clinical trials thyroid tumor rates were 1.3 versus 1.0 per 1,000 participant-years, with most cases having elevated calcitonin at baseline, and that the FDA required long-term monitoring in a cancer registry [1]. The label recommends not sharing pens between patients and says animal studies suggest possible fetal risk [2]. A 2025 meta-analysis assessed class-wide safety across 99,599 patients [12].

Liraglutide is an acylated GLP-1 analogue with 97 percent amino-acid sequence homology to human GLP-1(7-37). It activates the GLP-1 receptor, raising cyclic AMP in pancreatic beta cells and increasing insulin secretion in a glucose-dependent way [2]. A fatty-acid chain promotes albumin binding and gives a half-life of about 13 hours, allowing once-daily dosing [13][14]. Review literature describes how the discovery of GLP-1 and efforts to extend its short half-life led to liraglutide and then to semaglutide [14].

Novo Nordisk developed liraglutide after the discovery of GLP-1 and early efforts to extend its half-life; a 2019 review charts the discovery and development of liraglutide and, later, semaglutide [14]. The EU approved it in 2009 and the US in 2010 [1]. The LEADER trial reported cardiovascular outcomes in type 2 diabetes in 2016 and a renal-outcomes analysis followed in 2017 [15][16]. The SCALE program supported the weight-management product [6].

Liraglutide is mentioned less than semaglutide and tirzepatide. T Nation members describe using it for appetite control, getting it as Saxenda or from peptide sellers, and sometimes preferring it because of its shorter action [4][17][18]. One poster reports losing roughly 30 pounds and then regaining some after stopping [5], and another reports tiredness from low calorie intake and constant fullness [19]. Others mention insurance covering Victoza as a diabetes drug [20].

Liraglutide has an extensive randomized trial record. For weight, SCALE Obesity and Prediabetes, SCALE Diabetes, a 3-year prediabetes trial and STEP 8 (against semaglutide) are the main publications [6][7][8][3]. LEADER and a renal-outcomes analysis addressed cardiovascular and kidney outcomes in type 2 diabetes [15][16], LEAN tested liraglutide in non-alcoholic steatohepatitis [21], and a 2025 trial studied children aged 6 to under 12 with obesity [22]. A registered phase 2 study examined it in adolescents after sleeve gastrectomy [23]. No published trial has tested liraglutide for facial appearance.

lore.intro: In T Nation and similar forums liraglutide is treated as the older, shorter-acting GLP-1 option, mentioned alongside semaglutide for appetite control and cutting [4][5][18].

claims.claim: Liraglutide's shorter action lets users dose around cravings.
It is milder and less potent than semaglutide.
Liraglutide spares muscle better than other GLP-1 drugs.
Low calories plus constant fullness make training a chore.
Peptide-site liraglutide is an equivalent substitute for prescribed Saxenda.

timeline.event: SCALE trial of 3.0 mg for weight management published [6].
